processing: A prepared drink, not a leaf style: roasted rice is simmered in hard water, combined with sanpin-cha or bancha, and whisked in a big wooden bowl into a tall, stable foam.
harvest_season: Not tied to a harvest, since it is made to order from ordinary sanpin-cha or bancha.
appearance_dry: There is no dry product of its own; the ingredients are ordinary tea leaf and roasted rice.
appearance_liquor: A bowl of tea with a little red rice in it, topped by a white dome of foam and roasted peanuts.
appearance_wet: No leaf reaches the bowl; the foam holds its shape like soft-serve ice cream.
taste_profile: Toasty rice foam over mild tea, with roasted peanut on top and red rice underneath; it is as much about the airy texture as the flavour.

brewing.notes: Hard water matters: it is what lets the foam last. Simmer roasted rice in it, combine with the tea in a wide bowl and whisk with long straight strokes near the side, not in circles. Tea measures are an approximate starting point.

vintage_note: Not sold by year or season, because it is prepared on the spot from everyday tea. You meet it at cultural demonstrations and specialist tea sittings in Okinawa, and the tea going into it is whatever is current.
description:
Bukubuku-cha is Okinawa's whisked foam tea, and the foam is the point. Tea sits in the bowl with a spoonful of red rice, and a mound of white froth is piled on top, then finished with roasted peanuts.

The froth comes from rice, not from the tea. Roasted rice is simmered in the island's hard, limestone-and-coral water, mixed with sanpin-cha or bancha in a wooden bowl about 25 cm wide, and whisked with an oversized bamboo whisk over 20 cm long. With the right water, the foam can reportedly stand for an hour. The roast and strength of the rice matter a great deal.

There is no spoon. You open wide and draw the foam in from the top, and if it clings, you tap the bottom of the bowl. Making it at home in soft water is the classic mistake, since the foam collapses quickly. Keep your whisk in straight lines near the bowl's side; centre whisking and curved strokes yield less foam.

You cannot really buy it as a packet of leaf. Look for a demonstration or a tea sitting in Okinawa. One bowl whisks enough foam for several people, which sets it apart from other Japanese frothed teas.

If you enjoy the idea, compare it with other furi-cha, the frothed folk teas of Japan, such as Tokunoshima's fui-cha.
history:
One account traces it to the rice-flour substitute used at the Kitano tea gathering of 1587, said to have reached Ryukyu and been shaped into this drink at court, where it served to entertain Chinese envoys. That origin is not established. Firmer evidence comes from 1757, when a shipwrecked Ryukyuan crew's account recorded older women in Ryukyu drinking whisked sencha.

It faded in the Meiji era, though people in Naha still enjoyed it, and after the Second World War it survived only with a few market vendors who took orders. The custom then lapsed. Efforts to reconstruct it began in the late 1950s, and enthusiasts had restored it by about 1980.

A preservation society was founded in 1992. In March 2025 Japan's Agency for Cultural Affairs recognised it as a "100-Year Food".
